 Her Husband Inherits $250,000 When His Mother Dies. She’ll Lose Her $1,029 SSI Check Even Though the Money Is in His Name
 Gerelyn Terzo Sat, November 7, 2026 at 5:32 PM MST 5 min read Quick Read 
 Deeming rules count a non-SSI spouse's assets as the SSI recipient's, so a $250,000 inheritance in his name alone can end her benefits. 
 The couple's $3,000 resource limit is checked on the first of each month, so she could lose about $12,000 a year in SSI. 
 Report the inheritance promptly and spend down on excluded items like a home or car; gifting money away can trigger up to 36 months of ineligibility. 
 Building a portfolio and living off one are two completely different skills, and almost nobody teaches the second. This problem is what The Definitive Guide to Retirement Income helps, and it is free today. Read more here. (Sponsor) 
 Take a 67-year-old woman collecting the maximum federal Supplemental Security Income (SSI) payment for 2027, which is $1,029 a month. Her husband doesn't receive SSI. When his mother dies, he inherits $250,000 in cash and puts it in a savings account in his name only. She figures her check is safe because she never inherited a dollar. 
 24/7 Wall St. She could lose the whole check anyway. Money one spouse receives can end a benefit the other relies on, even when the inheritance is kept in a separate account. 
 Why His Savings Account Counts as Her Money 
 SSI is based on financial need. Social Security retirement benefits work differently. You earn them through payroll taxes, and there is no limit on how much you can own while collecting them. SSI only goes to people with very little income and very few assets. 
 The rule that matters most here is called deeming. When an SSI recipient lives with a spouse who isn't eligible for SSI, that spouse's resources are treated as if they were hers, even if she has no access to the money. That means his savings account still counts against her. 
 Cash and bank accounts count as resources. The limit for a couple stays at $3,000 in 2027, even though payments rose with the 3.6% cost-of-living adjustment (COLA). That puts her household $247,000 over the limit.

 The Inheritance Can Stop Her Check Immediately 
 The process happens in two steps. Money that comes in during a month is first treated as income for that month. If it is still in the account on the first day of the next month, it counts as a resource. His income can also be deemed to her, so her check may shrink or disappear in the very month the inheritance comes in. 
 Social Security checks countable resources at the start of each month. If the couple has more than $3,000 at that point, she isn't eligible for SSI that month. Say her husband's inheritance arrives in March and the money is still there on April 1. She loses her April eligibility, regardless of whose name is on the account. 
 At the federal maximum, she loses $1,029 a month, or $12,348 a year, for as long as the money stays countable. State supplements and other income can change her exact amount. In many states, getting SSI also qualifies you for Medicaid, so losing the check can affect her health coverage too. 
 Spending Down the Right Way Versus the Costly Way 
 Report the change promptly. If you don't report an inheritance, Social Security usually finds out later and sends a bill for every month she was paid while she wasn't eligible. 
 Use the exclusions that are allowed. Some things don't count as resources: the home you live in, one vehicle used for transportation, household goods, and burial funds of up to $1,500 each. A non-SSI spouse's IRAs and work pensions are also excluded. Paying down the mortgage or replacing an old car at a fair price turns countable cash into property that doesn't count. 
 Keep every receipt. Spending reduces your resources as of the first of the following month. Your records prove when the household got back under $3,000. 
 Don't give the money away. Transferring cash to your kids or selling property to a relative at a discount can trigger an SSI penalty lasting up to 36 months if Social Security determines you did it to qualify for benefits. 
 That gift rule belongs to SSI and has its own test. Medicaid nursing-home coverage uses a separate five-year look-back, so don't mix the two up when planning. 
 For many couples, a $250,000 reserve easily makes up for $12,348 a year in SSI, and keeping much of the money may be the right choice. Just make that choice deliberately, before the first of the month comes in. State rules and each household's mix of income and assets can change the result, so it's worth a call to Social Security or an elder law attorney before any money is moved.
